query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a high‐purity hexagonal boron nitride (h‐BN) coating to the surfaces of dipping and plating equipment will reduce the corrosion by molten aluminum during the hot dip process.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard metal components (e.g., steel rollers and guide plates) used in plating equipment.
generation.intervention: Deposit or coat the metal surfaces with a well‐adhered layer of h‐BN before exposing the parts to high‐temperature molten aluminum.
generation.conditions: Continuous or cyclic exposure to high-temperature (typically around the melting point of aluminum) liquid aluminum in dipping operations.
generation.structural_mediator: The h‐BN layer forms a dense, chemically inert barrier with a layered structure that resists wetting and physical attack by molten aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The inherent low wettability and chemical inertness of hexagonal boron nitride should prevent direct contact between the metal substrate and aggressive molten aluminum, thereby reducing attack and erosion of the underlying material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated parts are expected to exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates (e.g., reduced weight loss and surface degradation) compared to uncoated parts, thus prolonging service life under typical hot-dip aluminum plating conditions.
generation.baseline: Identical metal parts without the h‐BN coating subjected to the same hot dip aluminum plating process.
generation.boundary: The protective effect may be limited if the coating integrity is compromised (e.g., through mechanical damage or insufficient adhesion) or if process temperatures exceed the stability window of the h‐BN layer; conditions outside typical plating parameters may yield different behavior.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal coating thickness, adhesion quality on metal substrates under thermal cycling, and long-term mechanical durability under repeated immersion in molten aluminum.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical metal parts that are typically used in the plating equipment. Apply a uniform h‐BN coating to one set while leaving the other set uncoated. Subject both sets to repeated immersion in molten aluminum at process-relevant temperatures for a fixed number of cycles.
measurements: Mass loss measurements to quantify corrosion rates.
Surface microscopy (e.g., SEM) to assess surface degradation and coating integrity.
Adhesion tests of the coating before and after exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the h‐BN coated parts do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion (e.g., less mass loss and fewer surface defects) compared to the uncoated parts under identical conditions, the hypothesis that the h‐BN coating provides protective benefits against molten aluminum corrosion is falsified.
